# `sha2` — specification

## Maturity

**Grade:** 2 · S2 E1 A1 H1 P2 · limited by scope (parity), performance (fastest in the field not measured) *(generated by `zig build gen-catalog`)*

**Scope:** parity — OpenSSL 4.0 / Zig std 0.16.0 SHA-2 family (surveyed 2026-09-30)

**Audit:** review 2026-10-26 · mutation 2026-10-26 (77/79, 2 eq) · src 392d044c36f8d037

**Downstream consumer:** no

**Where we are ahead:** of `std`, on a machine without SHA-NI, from two blocks up (1.24–1.40× in the module's own bench, not re-run here); pure Zig with the same declarations as std (including under std's `Hmac`/`Hkdf`); RustCrypto's AVX2 path is SHA-512-only, ours covers both word sizes (its README); 0.40–0.99× OpenSSL's EVP calls on every row, HMAC 0.52–0.54× (2026-10-26, *Speed*); since 2026-10-26 the SHA-NI and AVX2 paths are chosen at run time, as OpenSSL, Go and RustCrypto do, so a baseline-x86-64 build gets them. **Where we are behind:** SHA-512's SHA512-extension path (Intel, Arrow Lake and later; OpenSSL and CRYPTOGAMS have it), no NEON path of our own (we hand SHA-256 to std where std has SHA hardware; SHA-512 on arm64 is scalar), no SHA-512 hardware path (→ Backlog, already listed).

## What this module is, and what it is not

SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512, SHA-512/224 and SHA-512/256 (FIPS
180-4 §6.7), plus std's plain truncations `Sha256T192`, `Sha512T224` and
`Sha512T256`, all with the public declarations of `std.crypto.hash.sha2`'s
types of the same names, and a faster compression function on x86-64 without
SHA-NI: CRYPTOGAMS' SHA-NI and AVX2 assembly, chosen at run time (see
NOTICE), with a pure-Zig SIMD and scalar engine everywhere else. It is **not**:

- an HMAC or HKDF: std's generic `Hmac(H)` and `Hkdf(Hmac)` instantiate over
  these types unchanged (tested), so there is nothing to add;
- a multi-message (multi-buffer) hasher: every speed-up here is within one
  message.

## Algorithm

FIPS 180-4 §6.2 (SHA-256), §6.4 (SHA-512), §6.3/§6.5 (the truncated
SHA-224/SHA-384 with their own initial values, §5.3.2/§5.3.4), padding §5.1.

- **Constants.** `K` (§4.2.2, §4.2.3) and the initial values (§5.3) are
  computed at compile time from their definitions: the first 32/64 bits of
  the fractional part of the cube (`K`) or square (initial values) root of the
  first primes, as the exact integer root of `p · 2^(r·w)` (`fracRoot`).
  SHA-224's initial values are the low halves of SHA-384's (§5.3.2 lists
  exactly those numbers). A test pins the first and last entries of each
  table to the standard's printed values and checks that SHA-256's `K` are the
  high halves of SHA-512's.
- **Rounds.** Straight from §6.2.2 step 3 / §6.4.2 step 3, fully unrolled,
  with the eight working variables renamed per round rather than moved
  (`round`). Two rewrites, both identities over bits: `Maj(a,b,c) =
  ((a ^ b) & (b ^ c)) ^ b`, carrying `b ^ c` as the previous round's `a ^ b`;
  `Ch(e,f,g) = (e & f) ^ (~e & g)`, which LLVM lowers to `and`/`andn`/`or`.
  With BMI2 the rotations are `rorx`. `T1` is summed as `((h + W_t+K_t) + Ch)
  + Σ1`, putting the value that depends on `e` last.
- **Schedule, scalar.** §6.2.2 step 1 in a 16-word ring, computed inline
  between rounds (`compressScalar`).
- **Schedule, SIMD** (`scheduleSimd`). For `n` = 2 … `lanes` consecutive
  whole blocks (`lanes` = 8 for 32-bit words, 4 for 64-bit: one 256-bit
  vector), load each block's 16 words as `16 / lanes` row vectors, byte-swap,
  and transpose each `lanes × lanes` tile (log2(lanes) stages of block swaps,
  `@shuffle`) so vector `W[t]` holds word `t` of every block, one block per
  lane. Run the recurrence `W_t = σ1(W_{t−2}) + W_{t−7} + σ0(W_{t−15}) +
  W_{t−16}` on those vectors, add `K_t`, and store the `rounds × lanes` table;
  lanes past `n` duplicate the last block and are never read. Then each block
  runs the scalar rounds reading its column (`roundsFromTable`), in order,
  chaining the state. This is legal because the schedule is a function of the
  block alone. Intel's whitepaper vectorizes four words of ONE block per
  vector and needs a two-step fix-up for `σ1`'s distance-2 dependency; lane
  per block has no such dependency and serves both word sizes with one
  generic body.
- **Schedule, one block** (`compressOne`, SHA-256 only). A lone block
  (a short message, `final`'s padding block, each of HMAC's key pads) has
  no neighbours to share a schedule with. Words t..t+3 of the block sit in
  one 4-lane vector, and the next four are computed while the scalar rounds
  consume the current four (Intel's single-buffer form). σ1 reaches back
  only two words, so the upper half of a new vector depends on its lower
  half; σ1 is applied twice, first to words t−2 and t−1 (lanes 0, 1), then
  to the fresh t and t+1 (lanes 2, 3). SHA-512's lone block stays scalar,
  because there the vector form measured slower.
- **Truncated variants.** SHA-512/t's initial values (§5.3.6) are generated
  at compile time by the standard's own procedure: SHA-512 of the string
  `"SHA-512/t"` under SHA-512's initial values XORed with `0xa5…a5`. A test
  pins the first and last word of each to §5.3.6.1/§5.3.6.2. A digest that
  ends inside a word (224 bits of a 64-bit word size) takes that word's
  leading bytes.
- **CRYPTOGAMS SHA-NI** (`.cryptogams_shani`, SHA-256/224 only):
  `sha256_block_data_order_shaext`, generated and renamed like the AVX2
  path. It drives `sha256rnds2`/`sha256msg1`/`sha256msg2` on XMM
  registers, with `palignr`/`pshufb` (SSSE3) for the schedule's shifts and
  the byte swap. perlasm encodes these as `.byte` sequences, which keeps old
  assemblers happy. The loop counts blocks down with `decq`.
- **CRYPTOGAMS AVX2** (`.cryptogams_avx2`, `src/asm/`). Andy Polyakov's
  `sha256_block_data_order_avx2` / `sha512_block_data_order_avx2`, generated
  by `tools/gen_cryptogams.sh` from a pinned commit and renamed (NOTICE lists
  every change). It is the same code OpenSSL ships. It computes the schedule
  of two blocks at once in the two 128-bit halves of a ymm register,
  interleaved with the first block's rounds, and runs the second block's
  rounds from the stored `W + K`. The rounds use `rorx`/`andn` and `lea` for
  the adds, which keeps ports 1 and 5 busy where our Zig rounds leave them
  idle (see *Speed*). For an odd block count, the second lane loads from
  the function's own stack frame, never past the input.
- **Padding and length** (`final`): `0x80`, zeros, then the bit count as a
  64-bit (SHA-224/256) or 128-bit (SHA-384/512) big-endian integer. The byte
  counter has the counter's width, as in std; bits shifted out of `total_len
  << 3` are dropped, which only matters past the standard's own message-size
  bound.

## Dispatch

Per word size (`Engine(Word).defaultBackend`), first match wins:

1. **`.stdlib`** — 32-bit words, and std has SHA hardware for the target:
   x86-64 with SHA-NI **and** AVX2 (std's own condition), or arm64 with
   `sha2`; not under the C backend (std's condition too). Whole blocks are
   handed to a `std.crypto.hash.sha2.Sha256` whose public `s` field is set to
   our state and read back — std's `update` over whole blocks with an empty
   buffer is exactly its compression. std's SHA-512 has no hardware path on
   any target, so 64-bit words never take this.
2. **`.cryptogams_shani`** — 32-bit words, chosen at run time, when CPUID
   reports SHA and SSSE3.
3. **`.cryptogams_avx2`** — chosen at run time, when CPUID reports AVX,
   AVX2, BMI1 and BMI2 and XGETBV shows the OS saves YMM state.

   Both are compiled for any x86-64 ELF target under LLVM, whatever CPU
   model the build names: LLVM assembles the module-level assembly for every
   x86-64 model, as it does crc32's `pclmulqdq`. One CPUID pass fills both
   answers (`CpuPaths`). It is cached in an atomic, and idempotent, so
   racing threads store the same value. A target that names the features
   skips the check at compile time. The assembly is handed at most 2^20
   blocks per call: SHA-256's AVX2 code compares its loop end in 32 bits,
   and a single call whose remaining input is a multiple of 4 GiB stopped
   early with a wrong digest (reproduced 2026-10-26; the opt-in test
   `SHA2_BIG=1` holds it). This is an upstream defect (`my $a4=$T1;` is
   `%r12d` for SHA-256). OpenSSL ships the same generator; it has not been
   checked there. Not reported upstream (owner, 2026-10-26); the cap is the
   fix here. SHA-512's AVX2 code compares in 64 bits, and the SHA-NI code
   counts blocks down in a 64-bit register (audit 2026-10-26). ELF only, because
   the files use ELF directives and the SysV ABI; that also rules out
   Windows. x32 is excluded too (`@sizeOf(usize) == 8`): the code does
   64-bit pointer arithmetic. The symbols are `.weak` + `.hidden`, so two
   objects that both carry this module still link. The self-hosted backends are excluded, because they are for the
   edit loop. The assembly starts with `.att_syntax` so that `-femit-asm`,
   which prints Intel syntax, parses it. It does not switch back, because
   that would break any module-level assembly after it in an object build.
   A re-assembled emitted file restates Intel after the end marker; the
   recipe is in `tools/bench.zig`.
4. **`.simd`** — x86-64 with AVX2 named by the target, **and** the LLVM
   backend: in practice a non-ELF x86-64 target (macOS) built for an AVX2
   model. The self-hosted backends are excluded because they are for the
   edit loop only (every gate builds with LLVM) and were not asked to lower
   256-bit shuffles; a Debug build with `-fno-llvm` therefore takes
   `.scalar`, never a compile error.
5. **`.scalar`** — everything else, including evaluation at compile time
   (`@inComptime()`).

Within `.simd`, a run of ≥ 2 whole blocks goes through the SIMD schedule in
batches of up to `lanes`. A remaining single block, and every block `final`
compresses, goes through `compressOne` for SHA-224/256 and through
`compressScalar` for SHA-384/512. A full-width schedule for one block costs
more than either.

The `.cryptogams_*` paths make a baseline-x86-64 build as fast as a native
one, on a SHA-NI machine as on an AVX2 one. `.simd` stays compile-time only, because Zig 0.17 has no
per-function target features (checked 2026-10-26: the langref has none).

**Test-only switch.** `test_hooks.forced` exists only when `builtin.is_test`
(outside tests `test_hooks` is an empty struct), and overrides the backend so
one test run holds `.stdlib`, `.cryptogams_shani` and `.cryptogams_avx2`
(where the CPU has them), `.simd`
(where compiled) and `.scalar` to the
same vectors and to std. It is a module-level variable, read only in test
builds; no production path can see it.

## Constant-time contract

SHA-2 itself has no secret-dependent control flow or memory access, and this
implementation adds none: no table indexed by data, no branch on data, the
batch size and the scalar/SIMD choice depend only on the **length** of the
input. Lengths are public in every protocol this is used in (TLS records,
HMAC key/message sizes). That is the whole claim; it rests on reading the
code and on the ctgrind harness (`src/ctgrind_harness.zig`; see the Maturity card's `ct` line). When the input is secret (HMAC keys, HKDF
PRKs, TLS transcript secrets), the working state is Z3 storage in
`CONVENTIONS.md` §2.1's sense — the transform's internal state, not wiped,
exactly as std does not wipe it; the SIMD schedule table on the stack is the
same class, and so is the `W + K` area of CRYPTOGAMS' stack frame. The
assembly has no secret-dependent branch or memory index. Its branches test
the block count and the end of its constant table. The ctgrind harness
runs through the AVX2 path: the digest's taint reaches the witness
printer, and no context is attributed to the module or left unattributed
(2026-10-26). The SHA-NI path is NOT measured by ctgrind. valgrind runs on
the host CPU, which has no SHA-NI. Its claim rests on reading: no branch
except the block-count loop, and no memory index derived from data. The
SHA instructions are fixed-latency. The SHA-NI function writes nothing to
the stack but the saved `%rbp`; state and message stay in XMM registers
(read 2026-10-26), so its stack residue is only the Zig frames around it.
jwt's ReleaseFast stack probe (HMAC over this module, with a burn) ran clean
under `qemu-x86_64 -cpu max`, where HMAC-SHA-256 takes this path
(2026-10-26). The XMM/YMM registers keep the last block's values after
return, on both assembly paths (`vzeroupper` clears only the upper
halves); neither std nor OpenSSL clears them either.

## Limits and refusals

None beyond FIPS 180-4's: any length, any split of `update` calls, any
alignment (loads are unaligned; `@ptrCast` to `*align(1)` vectors).
`buf_len` is a `u8`, which holds both block sizes.

## Anchoring

- **External.** The FIPS 180-4 / NIST example messages (empty, `"abc"`, the
  448-bit and 896-bit strings) and one million `'a'` for all four digests;
  RFC 4231 test cases 1, 2, 6 and 7 for HMAC-SHA-256/384/512 through std's
  `Hmac`; RFC 5869 A.1–A.3 (PRK and OKM) for HKDF-SHA-256 through std's
  `Hkdf`. Every vector was cross-checked against CPython's `hashlib`/`hmac`
  (OpenSSL) when written, 2026-09-29. HKDF-SHA-384 has no RFC vectors; its
  expected PRK/OKM for A.1's inputs were computed with CPython's `hmac` — a
  foreign implementation — and the test also compares against std's
  HKDF-SHA-384.
- **Live, external.** `tools/interop.zig` (`zig build interop-sha2`) holds
  302 000 cases from a fixed seed to the system OpenSSL 3 libcrypto
  (`EVP_Digest`, `HMAC()`, the `EVP_PKEY` HKDF), measured on 3.5.5. The
  cases cover all six named digests and messages to ~20 KiB, with lengths
  weighted to the padding edges, fed in 0–8 `update` pieces, and one-shot.
  They also cover `peek` mid-stream, the three plain truncations against
  the leftmost bytes of OpenSSL's SHA-256/512, HMAC over five digests with
  0–300-byte keys weighted to the block edges, and HKDF-SHA-256/384. An
  empty HKDF IKM has no oracle, because OpenSSL refuses it. A deliberate
  one-byte fault in the harness turned 234 cases red, which shows the
  oracle can fail (2026-10-25).
- **Re-derived.** `std.crypto.hash.sha2`, an independent implementation, for
  every backend: every length 0 … 1024 one-shot and split at a block edge; 24
  lengths up to 64 KiB each fed in random pieces biased to block edges (±1,
  whole multiples); every SIMD batch size 1 … 2·lanes+1 behind every prefix
  length 0 … block−1; byte-at-a-time with `peek` after each byte; one million
  `'a'` in uneven pieces; and a `testing.fuzz` harness (arbitrary bytes, an
  arbitrary cut, all digests, all backends).
- **Dispatch.** A test fails if an x86-64 ELF LLVM build does not report
  the path a fresh CPUID pass says it should: `.cryptogams_shani` for
  SHA-256 on a SHA-NI CPU, `.cryptogams_avx2` on an AVX2 + BMI1/2 one. A
  regression that silently fell back is therefore red, not merely slower.
  That test re-derives its expectation from `detectCpuPaths` itself, so a
  second one holds `detectCpuPaths` to std's own native CPU detection
  (`std.zig.system.resolveTargetQuery`, which reads CPUID and XCR0 itself).
  A wrong AVX2 or SHA bit passed every other test (audit 2026-10-26).
- **SHA-NI under emulation.** The development CPU has no SHA-NI, so the
  whole test binary (ReleaseSafe) and the OpenSSL oracle (all 302 000
  cases) also ran under `qemu-x86_64 -cpu max` (QEMU 10.2.1 TCG), where
  SHA-256 takes `.cryptogams_shani`. A baseline-x86-64 probe chose
  `.cryptogams_shani` there, `.cryptogams_avx2` under `-cpu Haswell` and
  natively, and `.scalar` under `-cpu qemu64` (no AVX). Every choice agreed
  with std (2026-10-26).
- **Long runs.** 40 000 blocks in one call (past the 21-bit product a
  careless `@min` gave, which hung the first chunking draft; the test kills
  that mutant), and 2^20 + 3 blocks one-shot against 1 MiB pieces.
- **Bounds.** Runs of 1–17 whole blocks are placed against a guard page,
  first at the tail and then at the head (`testkit.guard`), for every
  backend. A read past the last block or before the first faults instead of
  agreeing with std (2026-10-26).
- **Not exercised on real hardware here:** `.stdlib` as the *default* (no
  SHA-NI on the development CPU; the delegation itself is tested by forcing
  it, where std runs its scalar code) and the arm64 build.

**Anchor grade:** class B · oracle EXTERNAL

### Audit 2026-10-03

Reviewed `src/root.zig` whole (947 lines) against FIPS 180-4: padding (the
`0x80` byte, the spill to a second block exactly when fewer than `len_bytes`
bytes remain, the big-endian bit count), the buffering in `update` (every
partial/whole/partial split, `buf_len` as `u8`), the derived constants and
initial values (`fracRoot` stays inside `u256` for both word sizes), the
rounds, both schedules, the transpose and its masks, the batch loop in
`compressSimd` (a remainder is 0 or 1 block, so `compressScalar` reads a whole
block), the `.stdlib` hand-over to std's `update`, and the layout cast of the
`[rounds]V` table to `[rounds][lanes]Word`. No defect found. The
constant-time statement holds on reading: every branch and every batch size
depends on the input length only. INFO: `final` leaves the last partial block
and the padding in `buf` and the chaining state in `s` (documented under
*Constant-time contract*, same as std).

Mutation run (schemata, ReleaseSafe, one binary, baseline 1 s): **54 mutants,
52 killed, 2 equivalent, 0 real**. Covered: every branch and bound of `update`
and `final` (partial-buffer guard and take, early-return length, whole-block
split, padding threshold at both edges, `0x80`, the two zero fills, bit-count
shift and byte order, digest byte order, `init`); `compressBlocks` loop and the
`.stdlib` state hand-back; `compressSimd` batch threshold, batch size, block
count, trailing lone block; `scheduleSimd` lane clamp, byte swap, both
recurrence distances, `K` addition, transpose stage; every rotation/shift
amount of `sigma0/1`, `vsigma0/1`, `Σ0`, `Σ1`, `vrotr`; `Ch`, `Maj` and its
carried `b ^ c` (both compressors), the working-variable update, `T1` terms, the
final state addition (both compressors), the schedule start round, the big-endian
word load, the table column. Not mutated: the comptime constants (`K`, initial
values, `maskLow`/`maskHigh`), which are evaluated at compile time; any wrong
`K` entry, initial value or mask changes every multi-block digest and fails the
FIPS known answers.

Equivalent:
- `d.total_len +%= take` instead of `b.len` in `update`'s early return: that path
  is taken only when the whole input fits the buffer, so `take == b.len`.
- `compressSimd` loop `>= block_len` instead of `>= 2 * block_len`: a lone block
  through the lane-wide schedule (`n = 1`, padding lanes ignored) gives the same
  state; the threshold is a speed choice only.

### Audit 2026-10-26

The source changed since 2026-10-03: CRYPTOGAMS' assembly, the run-time
dispatch, SHA-512/t and the plain truncations, and `compressOne`. Reviewed
`src/root.zig` whole and both `src/asm/` files at the Zig/assembly boundary.
- **Regeneration.** `tools/gen_cryptogams.sh` reproduces both `.s` files
  byte for byte (upstream files pinned by commit and SHA-256).
- **ABI.** The functions follow SysV: callee-saved GPRs are pushed and
  restored, `%rsp` is restored from `%rbp`, and the AVX2 paths end with
  `vzeroupper`. They start with `endbr64`. The constant tables are
  64-byte aligned for the aligned loads.
- **CPU features.** The SHA-NI function uses only SSE2, SSSE3 (`pshufb`,
  `palignr`) and SHA instructions, which matches its SHA + SSSE3 condition.
  The AVX2 functions use AVX2, `rorx` (BMI2) and `andn` (BMI1), which
  matches AVX2 + BMI1 + BMI2 + XCR0 YMM.
- **Loop ends.** SHA-256 AVX2 has the 32-bit compare (above, capped).
  SHA-512 AVX2 compares in 64 bits. SHA-NI uses `dec %rdx` and runs at
  least one block; `compressBlocks` never passes 0.
- **Odd block.** For an odd block count the AVX2 code points its second
  lane at its own stack frame, never at the caller's memory (the guard-page
  test holds this).
- **Symbols.** All are `.weak`, `.hidden` and prefixed `zl_sha2_`.
- No defect found in the code.

Two instrument findings, both fixed:
- **No independent CPUID oracle.** Mutants that read the wrong AVX2 bit
  (bit 4 for 5) or the wrong SHA bit (28 for 29) passed every existing
  test. "The default backend" test re-derives from the same function, and
  a lost SHA-NI path merely drops out of the per-backend tests. The new
  test "CPU detection agrees with std's native detection" kills both.
- **The audit's source hash ignored assembly.** `moduleSrcHash`
  (`scripts/gates/gates.zig`) fingerprinted only `*.zig`, so regenerated
  assembly would not have made this audit stale. It now includes `*.s` and
  `*.S`.

Mutation run (schemata, ReleaseSafe, one binary per CPU model, baseline 3 s
native / 19 s under qemu): **25 mutants, 25 killed**. Each ran natively
(Kaby Lake: AVX2, no SHA-NI) and under `qemu-x86_64 -cpu max` (SHA-NI). The
dispatch mutants also ran in a `-mcpu=baseline` build, where AVX2 too is
decided at run time.
- `update` / `final`: partial-buffer guard, early-return length,
  whole-block guard, padding threshold, `0x80`, bit-count shift, the
  SHA-512/224 tail's leading bytes.
- Dispatch: the CPUID cache's known flag, the AVX2 and SHA bits, SHA-NI
  without its SHA condition, SHA-NI not preferred, SHA-NI taken for
  SHA-512, AVX2 not taken, SHA-NI and AVX2 calls swapped.
- `compressBlocks`: no 2^20 cap, a `u21` step, `.stdlib` state hand-over.
- Zig engine: lane clamp, `Maj`, `Ch`, schedule distance, `compressOne`'s
  σ1, the lone trailing block (SIMD and scalar).

Several kills depend on the CPU, so a single machine does not see all of
them:
- The known flag: under qemu, or in the baseline build.
- The SHA bit, SHA-NI preference and SHA-NI for SHA-512: on a SHA-NI CPU
  only.
- SHA-NI without SHA, and the swapped calls: on a CPU without SHA-NI only.
- The 2^20 cap: only through the opt-in 4 GiB test (`SHA2_BIG=1`, 2026-10-26).

Not mutated: the assembly itself (any change to its rounds or constants
fails the FIPS answers and the OpenSSL oracle) and the comptime constants.

## Speed

Comparative: `tools/bench.zig` (`zig build bench-sha2`) against OpenSSL
3.5.5's EVP digests and one-shot `HMAC()`, by user-mode cycles. The card's
numbers come from a JCC-mitigated build of the program, made with the
two-stage recipe in `modules/sort/tools/README.md`. The 2026-10-26 run,
5 rounds, backend `.cryptogams`, in ours/OpenSSL:

| rows | ratio |
|---|---|
| SHA-256 64 / 256 / 1 KiB / 16 KiB / 1 MiB | 0.49 / 0.68 / 0.88 / 0.97 / 0.99 |
| SHA-384 same sizes | 0.40 / 0.63 / 0.82 / 0.97 / 0.99 |
| SHA-512 same sizes | 0.40 / 0.63 / 0.82 / 0.97 / 0.98 |
| SHA-224 1 KiB · SHA-512/256 1 KiB | 0.87 · 0.82 |
| HMAC-SHA-256/384/512, 256-byte message | 0.52 / 0.54 / 0.54 |

The block function is OpenSSL's own, so bulk converges on 1.0. The rest of
the lead is EVP's per-call context handling, about 1 200 cycles per call.

Why the assembly, measured 2026-10-25/26 per block in a dependent chain
(`perf stat`, Kaby Lake, cycles):

| | SHA-256 | SHA-512 |
|---|---:|---:|
| CRYPTOGAMS AVX2, 1 block / bulk | 545 / 497 | 776 / 672 |
| our Zig, 1 block / bulk | 775 / 570 | 968 / 780 |
| our Zig rounds alone (no schedule) | 526 | 651 |

For the same ~1 800 instructions per SHA-256 block, our Zig rounds alone
run at 3.0 IPC; the assembly runs the whole block, schedule included, at
3.5. Three attempts to get there in Zig failed. They were a software
pipeline of the next batch's schedule between the rounds, the one-block
schedule for every block, and reordering the round so that `d += T1` comes
first. The vector schedule shares ports 0, 1 and 5 with the scalar ALU, so
it does not run "beside" the rounds for free; the assembly's `lea` adds use
ports the compiler's `add`s leave contended.

Table and machine for the std comparison in the README. Instruction counts from the ReleaseFast
build (2026-09-29): one round is 24 instructions (6 `rorx`, no spills); the
scalar schedule adds ~13 per word; the SIMD schedule costs ~1 670 vector
instructions per batch, i.e. ~5 per round per block at full width. The model
"instructions per block / 4 per cycle" predicts the measured ratios (1.29–1.33
for SHA-384 over long inputs, 1.24 at 1 KiB where one of nine blocks is the
lone padding block), which is why lone blocks are left scalar: an in-block
vector schedule would save about one instruction per word.

## What is deliberately not done

- **SHA-NI kernel of our own** — not now: std already uses SHA-NI when the
  target has it, and this module defers to std there (`.stdlib`). A kernel of
  our own could only be tested on a CPU this project does not have.
- **AVX-512 (`vprorq`, 16/8 lanes)** — not now: no consumer CPU with it.

## Open

- The speed-up for qap's TLS handshake has not been measured. Transcript
  updates and HMAC/HKDF calls are mostly lone blocks: 545 vs std's ~820
  cycles each. Measure there before claiming a handshake gain.

## Backlog / deferred

- **SHA512 extension (x86).** CRYPTOGAMS has had a SHA512-extension path
  since 2023. It needs Arrow Lake or later, and neither the development CPU
  nor QEMU 10.2's TCG runs it, so it would ship untested. Revisit when a
  runner or emulator has it.
- **SHA-NI speed is not measured.** The path is verified for correctness
  under emulation only. Measure it on a SHA-NI machine (CI's AMD runners)
  before quoting a speed.
- **(survey 2026-09-30) Priority of the two existing items:** SHA-512/256 and SHA-512/224 first: done 2026-10-25, together with std's three plain truncations. Run-time dispatch second: done 2026-10-26 for SHA-NI and AVX2 (CRYPTOGAMS, owner's choice of route).
- **Owner 2026-10-25/26: route for the bulk gap.** Our own Zig rounds could
  not reach OpenSSL's IPC (*Speed*). The owner chose CRYPTOGAMS' assembly
  over a separate session of round tuning.
- **NEON/SVE2 or SHA3-extension SHA-512 path for arm64** (survey 2026-09-30): RustCrypto has `aarch64-sha3` for SHA-512; here arm64 SHA-512 is scalar. Effort M, and untestable without arm64 hardware in CI (see SPEC's SHA-NI reasoning). Fits §2.
